title: Judge rightly (John 7:1–24)
hook: at the harvest festival of booths, he teaches in secret then openly

segments.voice: Yesterday, many walked away, and Peter said: Lord, to whom shall we go? Your line was to whom else? What did you stay with? Day six hundred twelve.

Each autumn, Jewish families who keep Sukkot build a little hut. Walls of wood or cloth, a roof of branches loose enough to see the stars through. For a week, they eat in it, and some sleep in it. It's called a sukkah, a booth, and the festival is Sukkot, the Feast of Tabernacles. Jews still keep it today. Today's chapter of John opens as that feast approaches, and Jesus's own brothers are pushing him: go up to Jerusalem, show yourself to the world.
screen: `A HUT WITH A ROOF OF BRANCHES.`

segments.voice: John says it plainly: "Now the Jews' feast of tabernacles was at hand." Tabernacle is an old word for a tent. The law of Moses told Israel to live in booths for seven days, remembering the years in the wilderness, when God's people lived in tents and God kept them. It was also a harvest festival, the end of the year's gathering, full of joy. Jesus's brothers want him to go and make a splash, and John adds a line that's honest about family: "For neither did his brethren believe in him." Jesus tells them his time hasn't come, and stays behind. Then, after they leave, he goes up anyway, quietly, not openly. Meanwhile in Jerusalem, people are whispering about him. He's a good man. No, he's leading people astray. Halfway through the feast, he walks into the temple courts and starts teaching out loud. People are amazed: "How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?" He hasn't studied under any teacher they know. He's from Galilee. They're judging by appearances, and he knows it. Then he takes up the old argument about the healing on the sabbath. You circumcise a baby boy on the sabbath, he says, when the eighth day falls on it, so the law of Moses isn't broken. Then why are you angry with me for making a whole man well on the sabbath? It's a careful argument from inside Jewish practice. And he ends with the line this day is named for: "Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment." Look past the surface. A man from Galilee with no teacher might be a teacher. A healing on the sabbath might be keeping the sabbath, not breaking it.
screen: then, large: `JUDGE NOT ACCORDING TO THE APPEARANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look beneath appearances. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've judged quickly. Maybe by their clothes, their accent, their job, or a single thing they said. Picture them clearly. Now try to imagine what you don't know. What they carry. What they've survived. What they might be good at. Let your picture of them get a little bigger. If you pray, you can ask to see them as God sees them. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with more curiosity than you did a minute ago. The bell holds the time.
Feast of Tabernacles. Sukkot, the autumn harvest festival when Jewish families live in booths, remembering the wilderness. Jesus teaches openly in the temple during it.
Your line: judge not by appearance. Today, when you catch yourself sizing someone up, ask one question you don't know the answer to. Day six hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Christians read this chapter as part of John's story of Jesus at the great Jewish feasts; Jews today keep Sukkot each autumn by building and eating in a sukkah.

original.note: Greek: tent-pitching. John's word for the Feast of Tabernacles, Hebrew Sukkot.

trapdoor: what you thought: a general warning not to be judgmental.
what it means: people judge Jesus by his background, and he asks them to look past the surface to what's really happening.
what a scholar hears: his argument from circumcision on the sabbath reasons from a lesser case to a greater, a style of argument Jewish teachers also used.

notes: Index word is 'Feast of Tabernacles'; index title 'Judge rightly'. Both kept.
Circumcision on the eighth day overriding the sabbath was accepted practice (cf. Mishnah Shabbat 18:3–19:2). The 'lesser to greater' (qal vahomer) argument style: confirm the trapdoor.
Jesus described as 'a craftsman from Galilee' (tekton, Mark 6:3; John itself doesn't name his trade). Changed in review from 'builder', since carpenter/builder/craftsman is debated. Confirm.
Hook (from index) says 'he teaches in secret then openly'; John 7:10 says he went up in secret, then taught openly (7:14). Voice and fork are accurate; consider rewording the index hook.

'His brothers': churches understand Jesus's brothers differently (Catholic: cousins or relatives; Orthodox: Joseph's children from an earlier marriage; many Protestants: younger sons of Mary). The script doesn't explain this; consider whether a note is needed.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced pilgrim crowds and booth-filled hillsides; cut 'a craftsman from Galilee' (John doesn't name his trade) and 'the kind teachers made'; 'teasing' changed to 'pushing' (7:3–4); 'Jewish families build' narrowed to families who keep Sukkot.
